scope: Style fidelity of the saved outputs, assessed separately from compression, cost, and plot fidelity. Both saved Anthropic variants are included; Opus has no completed Gatsby I output.
method: Source-aware close reading by the coding assistant, not blinded or independently judged. Examples were selected after generation to make observed differences inspectable. Existing five-gram measurements describe wording reuse, not a percentage of style preserved. No new model calls.
findings: For closeness to the authors’ style as these drafts stand, Opus and Sonnet generally lead the two GPT drafts. My earlier preference for Astra was an overall abridgment judgment that included compression and continuity; it should not be read as a finding that Astra sounds most like the originals.

The Anthropic approach is predominantly deletion and splicing: it retains the original clause structures, characteristic word choices, repetition, punctuation, and stretches of dialogue. GPT preserves recognizable signature passages but more often rewrites the surrounding prose into concise narration. The stylistic gap appears most clearly in that surrounding prose, not in famous quotations everyone preserved.

The length difference is substantial. In Gatsby I, Sonnet keeps about 95% of the source word count, compared with roughly half for either GPT draft. Across the three chapters with all four outputs, Opus retains about 73–75% of source length; Sonnet about 60–75%; GPT about 51–54%. These results cannot tell us which model would preserve style best at equal compression.

For Fitzgerald, Anthropic more consistently preserves Nick’s imaginative detours, hedges, musical accumulation, and the characters’ social performance in dialogue. Astra and Sol often preserve the observation or information while shortening the act of noticing or speaking that gives it its flavor. Astra has a modest stylistic edge over Sol in Gatsby I, but Gatsby II contains offsetting choices rather than a decisive GPT winner.

For Melville, Anthropic retains more of Ishmael’s digressive address, mock scholarship, classical/biblical allusions, and long winding syntax. Opus is my preferred stylistic version across the two Moby-Dick samples, although it is longer. Sol can be closer than Astra in local cadence: it preserves the enumerated wait and the full imaginary-writer quotation in The Carpet-Bag.

Verbatim language can still lose its stylistic function. Both Anthropic Loomings drafts and Sol retain the perdition punchline after cutting its money/heaven premise. Astra better preserves that joke as a working piece of religious irony. Likewise, Opus and both GPT drafts retain the tears-of-orphans climax in The Carpet-Bag, which Sonnet omits. Phrase overlap alone misses these losses.

All models retain meaningful authorial identity. The GPT drafts keep major signature passages, distinctive first-person narration, archaic vocabulary, and the ambiguous endings. Their weakness is unevenness: strongly preserved passages alternate with plainer compressed narration. The evidence supports an Anthropic advantage in surface style, a mixed Astra–Sol comparison, and no reliable equal-length model ranking.

chapter_judgments.judgment: Sonnet is closest, helped greatly by retaining nearly the whole chapter. Astra is closer than Sol in several narratorial and diction details. Opus unavailable.
Both Anthropic drafts preserve more texture. No decisive Astra–Sol winner: Astra keeps more imagery in places; Sol preserves more of some dialogue.

Opus best preserves the larger digressive movement; Sonnet retains much local rhetoric. Astra preserves an important joke’s logic better than the other three. Neither GPT retains the same classical texture.
Opus gives the best combination of source cadence and satirical payoff. Sol has several local stylistic advantages over Astra. Both GPT drafts preserve a climax lost by Sonnet.

examples.title: Nick’s imaginative detour becomes a location update
examples.interpretation: Both Anthropic drafts retain Fifth Avenue’s pastoral weather and the imagined flock of white sheep. Both GPT drafts reduce this to Nick trying to leave on Fifth Avenue. The scene still advances, but Nick’s fanciful way of seeing the city disappears.

examples.title: Qualified, playful speculation becomes a firmer statement
examples.interpretation: The source and both Anthropic drafts say ‘Evidently some wild wag of an oculist’. Astra retains ‘wild wag’ but removes ‘Evidently’; Sol removes both. These are small changes with a stylistic effect: Nick’s amused conjecture becomes more matter-of-fact narration. The elaborate image of the disembodied eyes remains in all versions.

examples.title: A speech’s social performance becomes a summary of its content
examples.interpretation: The source’s repeated ‘I’m going to’ and ‘I’ve got to’, the address ‘My dear’, and the extended shopping list stage Myrtle’s affected importance. Opus and Sonnet retain most of that performance. Both GPT versions report her promises and list in narration. Their details are largely faithful, but the reader hears less of Myrtle herself.

examples.title: The seduction of Nick’s attention survives more fully in Astra
examples.interpretation: Sonnet retains the source almost verbatim. Astra keeps ‘ceasing to compel my attention, my belief’, preserving the movement from attraction to distrust. Sol removes that intermediate movement and goes directly from the end of Daisy’s voice to Nick’s judgment of insincerity. The conclusion is the same, but the narrator’s changing state receives less expression.

belief, I felt the basic insincerity of what she had said. It made me

exact a contributory emotion from me. I waited, and sure enough, in a

examples.title: Melville’s comedy includes the classical contrast
examples.interpretation: All four retain the long ‘Whenever’ sequence and the pistol-and-ball line. Opus and Sonnet also retain Cato’s theatrical suicide contrasted with Ishmael quietly taking ship. Both GPT drafts cut that contrast. The plot does not require Cato, but the learned reference and deliberately anticlimactic answer are part of Ishmael’s comic voice.

passages.label: Original
passages.text:
Call me Ishmael. Some years ago—never mind how long precisely—having
little or no money in my purse, and nothing particular to interest me
on shore, I thought I would sail about a little and see the watery part
of the world. It is a way I have of driving off the spleen and
regulating the circulation. Whenever I find myself growing grim about
the mouth; whenever it is a damp, drizzly November in my soul; whenever
I find myself involuntarily pausing before coffin warehouses, and
bringing up the rear of every funeral I meet; and especially whenever
my hypos get such an upper hand of me, that it requires a strong moral
principle to prevent me from deliberately stepping into the street, and
methodically knocking people’s hats off—then, I account it high time to
get to sea as soon as I can. This is my substitute for pistol and ball.
With a philosophical flourish Cato throws himself upon his sword; I
quietly take to the ship. There is nothing surprising in this. If they
but knew it, almost all men in their degree, some time or other,
cherish very nearly the same feelings towards the ocean with me.

examples.title: Preserving a punchline is insufficient
examples.interpretation: Astra preserves the beliefs about money and heaven that motivate the cheerful-perdition joke. Opus, Sonnet and Sol cut that premise while retaining the punchline. Astra is stylistically stronger in this local unit despite its lower overall wording overlap: it preserves the ironic mechanism, not just Melville’s concluding words.

passages.label: Original
passages.text:
Again, I always go to sea as a sailor, because they make a point of
paying me for my trouble, whereas they never pay passengers a single
penny that I ever heard of. On the contrary, passengers themselves must
pay. And there is all the difference in the world between paying and
being paid. The act of paying is perhaps the most uncomfortable
infliction that the two orchard thieves entailed upon us. But _being
paid_,—what will compare with it? The urbane activity with which a man
receives money is really marvellous, considering that we so earnestly
believe money to be the root of all earthly ills, and that on no
account can a monied man enter heaven. Ah! how cheerfully we consign
ourselves to perdition!

examples.title: A cadence becomes arithmetic in Astra
examples.interpretation: The source and Anthropic drafts enumerate ‘a night, a day, and still another night’, making the wait unfold in the sentence. Sol largely retains the enumeration. Astra changes it to ‘two nights and a day’. The duration is accurate, but the rhetorical pacing is less close to Melville. All versions retain the anxious-grapnels pocket metaphor.

passages.label: Original
passages.text:
Now having a night, a day, and still another night following before me
in New Bedford, ere I could embark for my destined port, it became a
matter of concernment where I was to eat and sleep meanwhile. It was a
very dubious-looking, nay, a very dark and dismal night, bitingly cold
and cheerless. I knew no one in the place. With anxious grapnels I had
sounded my pocket, and only brought up a few pieces of silver,—So,
wherever you go, Ishmael, said I to myself, as I stood in the middle of
a dreary street shouldering my bag, and comparing the gloom towards the
north with the darkness towards the south—wherever in your wisdom you
may conclude to lodge for the night, my dear Ishmael, be sure to
inquire the price, and don’t be too particular.

examples.title: Mock scholarship needs its change of voice
examples.interpretation: Opus, Sonnet and Sol retain the elaborate direct quotation attributed to the imaginary old writer, including ‘thou observest’ and ‘the wight Death’. Astra keeps several archaic words but compresses the quotation into attributed narration. Sol better retains the distinct quoted voice and its winding syntax here; Anthropic additionally retains more of Ishmael’s commentary around it.

passages.label: Original
passages.text:
It was a queer sort of place—a gable-ended old house, one side palsied
as it were, and leaning over sadly. It stood on a sharp bleak corner,
where that tempestuous wind Euroclydon kept up a worse howling than
ever it did about poor Paul’s tossed craft. Euroclydon, nevertheless,
is a mighty pleasant zephyr to any one in-doors, with his feet on the
hob quietly toasting for bed. “In judging of that tempestuous wind
called Euroclydon,” says an old writer—of whose works I possess the
only copy extant—“it maketh a marvellous difference, whether thou
lookest out at it from a glass window where the frost is all on the
outside, or whether thou observest it from that sashless window, where
the frost is on both sides, and of which the wight Death is the only
glazier.” True enough, thought I, as this passage occurred to my
mind—old black-letter, thou reasonest well. Yes, these eyes are
windows, and this body of mine is the house. What a pity they didn’t
stop up the chinks and the crannies though, and thrust in a little lint
here and there. But it’s too late to make any improvements now. The
universe is finished; the copestone is on, and the chips were carted
off a million years ago. Poor Lazarus there, chattering his teeth
against the curbstone for his pillow, and shaking off his tatters with
his shiverings, he might plug up both ears with rags, and put a
corn-cob into his mouth, and yet that would not keep out the
tempestuous Euroclydon. Euroclydon! says old Dives, in his red silken
wrapper—(he had a redder one afterwards) pooh, pooh! What a fine frosty
night; how Orion glitters; what northern lights! Let them talk of their
oriental summer climes of everlasting conservatories; give me the
privilege of making my own summer with my own coals.

Yet, as an old writer—of whose works I possess the only copy extant—says, it maketh a marvellous difference whether thou lookest out from a glass window where the frost is all outside, or from that sashless window where the frost is on both sides, and the wight Death the only glazier. Yes, these eyes are windows, and this body of mine is the house. But it’s too late to make improvements now. The universe is finished; the copestone is on, and the chips were carted off a million years ago.

passages.label: GPT-6.1 Sol
passages.text: It stood on a sharp bleak corner, where that tempestuous wind Euroclydon kept up its howling. Yet it is a mighty pleasant zephyr to any one in-doors, with his feet on the hob. “In judging of that tempestuous wind called Euroclydon,” says an old writer—of whose works I possess the only copy extant—“it maketh a marvellous difference, whether thou lookest out at it from a glass window where the frost is all on the outside, or whether thou observest it from that sashless window, where the frost is on both sides, and of which the wight Death is the only glazier.”

examples.title: The satirical climax matters more than an extra stretch of quotation
examples.interpretation: Opus and both GPT drafts preserve the ice palace and tears of orphans. Sonnet instead ends the Lazarus questions without that climax, then moves to the whaling transition. Sonnet’s very high wording overlap therefore does not guarantee preservation of the passage’s strongest satirical turn.

passages.label: Original
passages.text:
Now, that Lazarus should lie stranded there on the curbstone before the
door of Dives, this is more wonderful than that an iceberg should be
moored to one of the Moluccas. Yet Dives himself, he too lives like a
Czar in an ice palace made of frozen sighs, and being a president of a
temperance society, he only drinks the tepid tears of orphans.

passages.label: Opus 5.5
passages.text: But what thinks Lazarus? Can he warm his blue hands by holding them up to the grand northern lights? Yet Dives himself, he too lives like a Czar in an ice palace made of frozen sighs, and being a president of a temperance society, he only drinks the tepid tears of orphans.
